The old days

What TDD is, and why it works for humans

The old days

TDD myths

“TDD is writing the tests first”

“TDD is about testing”

“You don’t write ‘the tests’ first. You write a test first.”

Tim Ottinger

“TDD is not really about writing tests before code. It’s about using tests in short-lived RGR cycles as a tool to design code.”

Andrea Laforgia

“The tests that drive our design often correspond to good regression tests, but certainly not always.”

Jason Gorman

The screenshots are the original LinkedIn posts: people who teach TDD keep having to write about these misconceptions. All three come back later. Ottinger returns on the tiny-steps slide (GLM wrote all its tests up front). Laforgia returns on the charade slide (by his definition the agents did test-first, not TDD). Gorman returns on tiny steps and in mutation testing; he mutation-tests new code routinely.

The old days

The evidence for humans

40–90%

fewer pre-release defects in four industrial teams (Nagappan et al. 2008, Microsoft and IBM)

15–35%

more development time, as the teams themselves estimated it

→ Fucci et al. 2017: short, steady cycles mattered more than writing the test first

→ Ghafari et al. 2020: studies disagree mostly because they’re set up differently

Every step answers a human limitation. Which of them does an agent actually have?

Good but not unanimous: a big drop in defects, a real time cost, and studies that disagree mostly because they are set up differently. Add a story from your 12 years here. End on the question; it opens part 2.

Part 2

The new ways

What happened when agents were told to do TDD

21:00–36:00.

The new ways · An agent ≠ a human

Which of TDD’s benefits does an agent need?

It doesn’t have

Fear

Boredom

Discipline inconsistency

Context switching fatigue

Not knowing where the code is going

It has, as badly as us or worse

Misreading the spec

Blind spots in its own tests

Gold plating: Beck warns about unrequested features

GLM wrote the same misreading into its test and its code.

Callback to “which of them does an agent actually have?”. Gold plating is the human benefit that partly carries over: probity rejected two greens that went too far. Be fair: no run gold-plated this kata (14–32 lines of production code each).

The new ways

What others found

Birgitta Böckeler · Aug 2026

TDD prompts gave no quality gain, for 3–8.5× the tokens.

Emily Bache · Sep 2026

That tested a prompt, not TDD. A test list and a harness are what’s missing.

→ So I tested both: TDD by prompt, and TDD enforced by a harness.

Böckeler: “TDD inside the agent loop: theater or actual value?”, martinfowler.com, 10 Aug 2026. Bache: response video on Modern Software Engineering, 23 Sep 2026. Both are summaries, not quotes.

The new ways

The experiment

9 + 1

agent runs on the same kata: 9 told to do TDD, 1 told not to

2016

my own run, live in front of an audience

9

planted bugs via mutation testing, plus an acceptance suite the agents never saw

→ Every red and green replayed from the git history

Say it before anyone asks: n = 1 per setup, on a 20-line kata the models have seen many times. Two runs of the same model differed more (8 of 9 vs 5 of 9 planted bugs caught) than the process changed anything. Böckeler’s and Jain’s larger studies show the same pattern.

The new ways

Agentic TDD skills: it looks good, but it’s a charade

46%

of tests passed as soon as they were written (26 of 57): the agent already knew the answer

→ GLM: 7 of 7 genuine reds, every commit labelled correctly, and it ships “Josh wins 1 to 2”

→ Ten implementations, one design: a rank string, indexOf, two counters

→ On this kata, following TDD didn’t change the agents’ design. It only tidied it.

→ Reflections: one copied from another model, one cites commit hashes that don’t exist

46% is across the six agents told to do TDD by prompt. GLM returns “Josh wins 1 to 2” when Josh wins 2–1, and its own tests say that is correct: ask the room again what x was. Callback to Laforgia’s quote from the myths slide: by his definition (tests as a tool to design code), design the tests didn’t change isn’t TDD. The evidence: the run without any tests has the same design; the tidying is the next slide.

The new ways

Tiny steps aren’t meaningful for an agent

Fake it

Increases cycle speed for humans. An agent doesn’t need this detour.

Minimal steps

Lower a human’s risk. For an agent, they led to tests that drive the code, not tests that protect it.

Gorman called it

The tests that drive the design aren’t always good regression tests

“A test first, not the tests”

A human rule against overinvesting up front: GLM wrote all 7 tests first, as skipped tests. For an agent, that investment is cheap.

Callbacks to Gorman and Ottinger from the myths slide. Minimal steps choose examples that are enough to drive the code, which is not the same as enough to protect it: Opus 5, the most minimal-step run, caught 5 of 9 planted bugs. GLM on fake it: “TDD created a bug and then caught it”. GLM’s skipped tests: commit 0512a46, 7 skipped tests, 7 genuine reds. Beck’s reasons for one test at a time were human: rework, and the gloom of waiting for anything to pass.

The new ways

Enforcing TDD with a harness: probity

11 of 12

tests genuinely red

4

real refactors: the most faithful TDD in the repo

→ The same result as no TDD, at 13× the cost and 22× the time

→ It dropped the tests that couldn’t go red, so it caught fewer planted bugs: 6 of 9, against 7 of 9 without TDD

→ 9 of 13 blocks were false positives; resending the same edit usually got through

Callback to Bache: she said a harness was missing, so here it is. Probity 1.10.1 by Nizar Selander: a hook that blocks every production write unless an AI validator sees a failing test it addresses. It always enforces the smallest step, which is stricter than Beck’s TDD: callback to the Obvious Implementation planted in the demo. Bache was right that a harness improves adherence; it didn’t improve the result. One run, unattended, so Selander’s main claim (less hand-holding for an interactive human) went unmeasured.

The new ways

The cost: tokens, dollars and time

RunTimeCostPlanted bugs caught
No TDD · Opus 5.529 s$0.277 of 9
TDD by prompt · Opus 5, run 13 min 47 s$2.078 of 9
TDD by prompt · Opus 5, run 24 min 18 s$2.725 of 9
TDD enforced by probity · Opus 5.510 min 48 s$3.546 of 9

Small experiment: one run per setup, on an easy 20-line kata

8–13× the cost and 8–22× the time, with no measurable quality gain.

Measured from the session transcripts at list prices. Opus 5 costs $5/$25 per million tokens and Opus 5.5 $4/$20, so TDD by prompt on Opus 5.5 would be about a fifth cheaper. In absolute terms the money is trivial next to an hour of developer time; the point is that nothing measurable came back for it. Two runs of the same model caught 8 of 9 and 5 of 9. On bigger problems: more cycles, each resending a larger context, so the overhead grows (Opus: “It scales with the ceremony, not with the difficulty”). Fair caveat: on an unfamiliar problem the benefit may grow too, because the agent no longer knows the answer. On Jain’s much larger task the frontier model’s harness still cost about 7× for no quality gain.

The new ways · Naresh Jain, Oct 2026

Are harnesses worth the cost?

ModelHarnessAcceptedTimeCost
Sol (frontier)No10 of 106 min 51 s~$0.41
Sol (frontier)Yes10 of 1019 min 53 s~$2.68
Luna (cheap)No3 of 1015 min 56 s~$0.09
Luna (cheap)Yes10 of 1035 min~$0.27

→ His harness isn’t TDD: human-written specs and examples, plus an independent acceptance gate

The ceremony buys nothing for a frontier model on a task it can already do.

“Are Harnesses Worth the Cost?”, martinfowler.com, 13 Oct 2026. A greenfield Java backend-for-frontend, 10 runs per arm, judged by 178 external acceptance tests. The harness took the cheap model from 3 of 10 to 10 of 10, and harnessed Luna still cost about a third less than unharnessed Sol. His recommendation matches this talk: for frontier models, run the independent check once as a final gate; for cheaper models, run it throughout.

Part 3

The way forward

For the coming year

36:00–42:00. Seven slides in six minutes: keep moving. The buffer from dropping the herdr race covers the extra one.

The way forward

Leave behind

Fake it and minimal green

Forcing the smallest step

A perfect process as proof of quality

Red as the proof that a test can fail

→ Keep the proof, drop the ritual: mutation-test afterwards instead (Gorman, Böckeler)

For the agent, not for teaching humans. Fake it guards against a human’s premature generalisation; the agent already knows the target, so it manufactures intermediate bugs. Beck’s own TDD allows bigger steps when you are confident (Obvious Implementation).

The way forward

Planning

Why? To not have to redo, and to make sure interpretations are correct.

The ambiguity

GLM’s “Josh wins 1 to 2”: no agent’s TDD caught the “x to y” ambiguity.

One agreed example, “Josh wins 2 to 1”, would have caught it in seconds.

The expectations

Agreed with the team before the agent starts.

Astra’s were agreed with me first, and only its suite pins the “x to y” reading.

The agent turns them into its own test list.

A small step compared to spec-driven development (spec-kit, OpenSpec)

This talk was planned first

~92%

of the planned slides’ text is still the first generated version

Two lists that used to be one. The expectations (what must be true) are agreed with the team before the agent starts; Laforgia suggests writing them together, like a Specification by Example workshop. The test list (which unit tests, in what order) was the human’s working memory; it now belongs to the agent’s inner loop. Astra’s agreed plan also said “Read decks without modifying them”, but no test ever checked it: the gap that Expectation-Driven Development closes by making the agent prove each expectation. This talk as the example: we wrote and argued over the plan before generating any slides, and about 92% of the planned slides’ text (1,529 of 1,653 words) is still the first generated version. New requirements are left out: the three red/green/refactor slides imported from my old deck and the Expectation-Driven Development slide (with them included it is 80%). Measured per slide, so moving a slide is not a change; re-measure when the deck is final with python3 presentation/deck/measure-changes.py --exclude step-red,step-green,step-refactor,edd.

The way forward

Vertical slicing

→ Small diffs a human can actually review

→ Fast incremental delivery at all layers

From experience, not from this experiment

UI

API

Domain

Data

One slice through every layer

Be explicit that this one comes from experience: the kata is a single slice, so the experiment says nothing about it.

The way forward

Move up a loop

Outer loop

The human

Inner loop

The agent

The double loop from Growing Object-Oriented Software (Freeman & Pryce, 2009)

→ Outer loop, acceptance tests: the human

→ Inner loop, red/green/refactor: the agent

Isn’t this just ATDD/BDD again? Yes, and that’s the point.

We are not abandoning TDD; we are moving up a loop. The old ideas that survive are the outer loop.

The way forward

Use acceptance-test-driven examples to specify desired behaviour

This experiment

Only the acceptance suite the agents never saw caught GLM’s and Gemma’s bugs

Mathews & Nagappan 2024

Tests given with the task help LLMs

Konstantinou et al. 2026

14% vs 25%

faults found by tests written after faulty code vs. independent tests

→ Jain’s harness is the same idea, tested at scale

Examples are executable; a spec document isn’t.

GLM and Gemma had the same author for code and tests, so the same misreading sat in both; only an outside suite caught them. Mathews & Nagappan, “Test-Driven Development for Code Generation” (2024): supplying tests improves LLM success. Konstantinou, Tambon, Papadakis, “On the risk of coding before testing” (2026): tests generated after faulty code detect 14% of faults, against 25% for independently generated tests.

The way forward · Andrea Laforgia, Mar 2026

Expectation-Driven Development

1

Write the expectations in plain text, before any code

2

The agent proves each one with executed evidence, not a story about it

3

Critical paths become automated tests

“The fox can guard the henhouse if there’s a different fox checking the first fox’s work.”

Andrea Laforgia

His own caveat: not battle-tested yet

The same Laforgia as on the myths slide, three years on: his Substack post “Expectation-Driven Development” (21 March 2026) keeps TDD’s discipline of specifying behaviour before implementation, “without the ceremony”. Our data backs his two demands. Executed evidence, not narrated: our reflections show narrated evidence (one copied from another model, one citing commit hashes that don’t exist). A different fox: only the acceptance suite the agents never saw caught GLM’s and Gemma’s bugs. His expectations are plain language, unlike “examples are executable” on the previous slide; his executed evidence and tests make them executable later. He says himself he hasn’t battle-tested it on a real project.

Test-first becomes spec-first.

From Beck’s TDD by Example to Adzic’s Specification by Example.

The human owns the examples. The agent does the cycles.

42:00–44:00. The bookend: the old talk was called “TDD: By Example”.
